query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a high‐temperature stable, self‐lubricating secondary phase into the CoCrFeNi matrix will enable the alloy to form an adaptive tribofilm during sliding that maintains low friction and wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Monolithic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without any added secondary phase.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled dispersion of a self‐lubricating secondary phase that is stable and reactive across the full temperature range, enabling in situ tribofilm formation.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under variable loads and ambient or controlled atmospheres, spanning the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an adaptive, lubricious tribofilm at the sliding interface derived from the secondary phase particles.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the secondary phase is dispersed and provides a baseline friction reduction; as the temperature increases, its thermally activated transformation leads to the formation of a continuous lubricious tribofilm that reduces friction and wear by providing a shearable, protective layer against substrate abrasion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with the secondary phase will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across all tested temperatures compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics from the CoCrFeNi alloy without the secondary self‐lubricating phase.
generation.boundary: The improved performance is expected under moderate to high loads in environments that do not induce extreme oxidation or degradation of the lubricant phase; under excessive mechanical stresses or highly aggressive atmospheres, the tribofilm may become unstable.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by analogous behavior in other self-lubricating systems (e.g., formation of lubricious oxides at ~704 °C), the exact transformation kinetics, tribofilm stability under cyclic or extreme loads, and environmental sensitivities for the CoCrFeNi matrix remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another set with the incorporated self‐lubricating secondary phase. Subject both sets to standardized sliding tests (using a tribometer) across a temperature sweep from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled load and environmental conditions. Monitor the evolution and durability of the tribofilm using in situ surface characterization techniques.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature and load
Wear rate (e.g., volume loss, wear track depth)
Surface morphology and tribofilm formation (via microscopy and spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under the majority of test conditions (across the full temperature range), the CoCrFeNi sample with the secondary phase fails to show statistically significant reductions in both friction and wear rate relative to the baseline sample, or if the tribofilm does not form/stabilize as characterized by surface analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.
